did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 30 opens with a prophetic formula characteristic of the book of Ezekiel: “The word of the LORD came to me, saying,” emphasizing that the message was delivered to the prophet by the LORD.
Did you know? The prophecy describes the “day of the LORD” as “a day of clouds” and “a time of nations”—an expression referring to a day of calamity, war, and upheaval among the nations.

Did you know? Egypt is not the only nation mentioned in the prophecy: Cush, Put, Lud, Arabia, Kub, and “the people of the land of the covenant” are also included among the nations that will fall by the sword along with Egypt.

Did you know? The extent of the devastation is described by the words “from Migdol to Syene,” meaning throughout the land from north to south, according to the boundaries of the places mentioned in the verse.
Did you know? Ezekiel explicitly identifies Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as the one who will bring destruction upon Egypt, together with his army and the “ruthless nations.”
Did you know? Egypt’s defeat is also described as an attack on its water sources: the LORD says, “I will dry up the streams of the Nile,” and the land will be handed over to foreigners.

Did you know? The prophecy also includes a religious struggle: the LORD declares that He will put an end to the idols and images in Memphis, and that there will no longer be a prince from the land of Egypt.
Did you know? The chapter mentions additional Egyptian cities—On, Pi-beseth, Tahpanhes, and No—and describes falling by the sword, captivity, and darkness as signs of destruction.
Did you know? The latter part of the chapter contains a dated prophecy: it was given in the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh day of the month.

Did you know? Ezekiel uses the image of “arms” to describe political and military power: Pharaoh’s arms are broken, while the arms of the king of Babylon are strengthened; as a result, Egypt will be scattered among the nations.
